name: LNK564DN-TL
title: LinkSwitch-LP LNK562-564: off-line switcher IC with 700 V MOSFET for linear transformer replacement, up to 3 W
summary: LNK562, LNK563 and LNK564 put a 700 V power MOSFET and an ON/OFF controller on one die, for small isolated flyback supplies up to 1.9, 2.5 and 3 W that replace 50/60 Hz linear transformers. The chip powers itself from DRAIN, draws under 150 mW from a 265 VAC line at no load, jitters its switching frequency for EMI, and protects itself with auto-restart and hysteretic thermal shutdown. Tight current-limit trimming allows designs with no primary clamp at lower power. LNK564DN-TL is the 100 kHz, 3 W device in SO-8C on tape and reel.

notes: Order code: LNK, the series number 562, 563 or 564, the package letter (P plastic DIP, G plastic surface-mount DIP, D plastic SO-8), the lead-finish letter, then -TL for tape and reel. LNK564DN-TL is the 100 kHz, 3 W device in SO-8C on a reel.
Lead finish G (RoHS compliant, halogen free) is not recommended for new designs.
Tape and reel is offered for the G package (1 k pieces minimum) and the D package (2.5 k pieces); it is not offered for the P package.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: Off-line flyback with feedback taken from a primary-side bias winding. D1 on the line side and D2 on the neutral side rectify the AC input; L1 and the bulk capacitor C1 filter it, and the chip's DRAIN switches the primary of T1. D3 and C2 rectify and smooth the secondary for the DC output, with R1 across it. D4 and C3 rectify the bias winding, and the divider R2 over R3 feeds that voltage to FB. C4 decouples BYPASS.

parts.note: primary P1-P2, secondary S1-S2, bias B1-B2; P2, S1 and B1 are the dotted ends

notes: The output follows a constant-voltage line up to the rated point VR, IR, then folds back in current as the output voltage falls (operation topic 'Output envelope').

circuits.title: 6 V, 330 mA CV/CC linear replacement power supply
circuits.description: An adapter giving 6 V at 330 mA, regulated in voltage and then in current, on a 90-265 VAC input built on an LNK564PN with no primary clamp. D1 and D2 rectify the line, RF1 and L1 with the single bulk capacitor C1 filter it. The bias winding (pins 4-5) is rectified by the slow diode D3 and smoothed by C3; R1 and R2 divide that voltage onto FB, and the chip skips cycles to keep FB at 1.69 V. The secondary (pins 7-6) feeds the ultra-fast D4 and C5; R3 preloads the output, VR1 can clamp it if the loop opens, and C4 is a Y capacitor from the secondary return to the primary return. C2 decouples BYPASS.

parts.note: primary 2-1, secondary 7-6, bias 4-5; 1, 7 and 4 are the dotted ends; a shield winding is tied to pin 2 with its other end open

notes: RF1, VR1 and C4 are optional parts.
With a sleeve over it, L1 can serve as the fuse as well as the filter; RF1 is the alternative fusing part.
D2 may be left out where less EMI margin and lower surge withstand are acceptable; D1 then has to be an 800 V diode.
Peak drain voltage stays below about 550 V at 265 VAC with no primary clamp, against the 700 V minimum BVDSS.

Below the FB auto-restart threshold (0.8 V on FB, about 1 V to 1.5 V at the output) the supply cycles 800 ms off and 100 ms on until the fault clears; the switching frequency falls to about 50% of its starting value before that point.
Average short-circuit output current is well below 1 A, and the output stage withstands a continuous short.
No-load input power is about 140 mW at 265 VAC with R3 fitted. Raising C3 to 0.47 µF or more, or R3 to 2.2 kΩ or more, lowers it further while the output stays well below its 9 V limit.

circuits.title: General test circuit
circuits.description: The bench circuit the electrical characteristics are measured in. A 50 V supply feeds DRAIN through switch S1 and a 470 Ω, 5 W resistor. FB is driven from an adjustable 0 to 50 V supply through switch S2 and 470 kΩ. BYPASS has 0.1 µF to the SOURCE pins, which are the common return.

operation.text: One die holds a 700 V power MOSFET and its controller: oscillator with frequency jitter, feedback sensing and logic, a 5.8 V regulator, BYPASS undervoltage detection, over-temperature shutdown, a current limit with leading edge blanking, and an auto-restart counter. Regulation is ON/OFF: each cycle is either switched or skipped, so there is no PWM loop and no compensation network.

The average switching frequency is 66 kHz (LNK562), 83 kHz (LNK563) or 100 kHz (LNK564). The oscillator produces a clock marking the start of each cycle and the DCMAX signal that caps the on time. The frequency is jittered by about 5% peak to peak at a 1 kHz rate to spread both average and quasi-peak EMI; the jitter is seen on a scope triggered on the falling DRAIN edge. A drain-voltage capture at fOSC marks the jittered period at 64 kHz and 68 kHz.

FB is a low-impedance source follower sitting at 1.69 V. When more than 70 µA flows into it the feedback logic goes low (disable). The logic is sampled on the clock edge at the start of each cycle: high means the MOSFET switches for that cycle, low means the cycle is skipped. Changes on FB later in the cycle have no effect.

Below 1.69 V on FB the oscillator frequency falls linearly, reaching typically 48% of fOSC at the 0.8 V auto-restart threshold. This limits output current when the output voltage drops below the regulation point VR, giving a constant-voltage region followed by a falling, current-limited region past the rated point VR × IR.

While the MOSFET is off, the regulator charges the BYPASS capacitor to 5.8 V from the DRAIN voltage; while it is on, the chip runs from the charge on that capacitor. Internal consumption is low enough that the chip runs indefinitely on current taken from DRAIN. 0.1 µF on BYPASS serves both as decoupling and as energy store. If current is fed into BYPASS from outside, a shunt clamps the pin at 6.3 V; feeding it through a resistor from a bias winding lowers no-load input power.
The MOSFET is held off when BYPASS falls below 4.85 V and stays off until BYPASS climbs back to 5.8 V.
Die temperature is sensed. At typically 142 °C the MOSFET is turned off, and it switches again only after the die has cooled by 75 °C (hysteretic, self-recovering).

When MOSFET current crosses ILIMIT the switch turns off for the rest of the cycle. For a time tLEB after turn-on the current-limit comparator is blanked, so that the spike from capacitance and rectifier reverse recovery does not end the pulse early.

A counter clocked by the oscillator is cleared each time FB rises above VFB(AR). If FB stays below VFB(AR) for over 100 ms, as in an output short or an open loop, switching stops; the part then turns switching on and off at a duty cycle of about 12% until the fault is gone. Delivered power in such faults falls by more than 85%.

Pulling FB low enables switching at the next DCMAX cycle start; tEN, at most 17 µs, runs from the FB fall to the first drain transition, and the cycle period is tP = 1/fOSC. The output disable setup time tDST is 0.5 µs typical.

The output power table assumes: a minimum DC bus of 90 V or more at 85 VAC, or 240 V or more at 230 VAC or at 115 VAC with a doubler, with input capacitance sized to hold it; a 6 V secondary with a Schottky rectifier; 70% efficiency; voltage-only regulation with no secondary current control; discontinuous conduction (KP > 1); a core large enough for a practical transformer (Table 2); SOURCE pins soldered to enough copper to hold them at or below 100 °C; 50 °C ambient for open frame and 60 °C inside an adapter enclosure.

For KP below 1 it equals primary ripple current divided by peak primary current; above 1 it is the ratio of MOSFET off time to secondary diode conduction time. Because of the flux-density limit for low audible noise, designs normally run discontinuous, which permits fast rather than ultra-fast output diodes and lowers EMI.

With no clamp, only the capacitance at the drain node limits the leakage spike, so peak drain voltage is set by the highest line voltage, VOR, the energy in the leakage inductance (set by that inductance and the peak primary current) and the capacitance of the primary winding. Leakage ringing lasts longer than with a clamp and can raise EMI. For universal or 230 VAC clampless designs: use them only up to PO ≤ 2.5 W with VOR ≤ 90 V; for PO ≤ 2 W wind a two-layer primary so its intra-winding capacitance is 25 pF to 50 pF; for 2 W < PO ≤ 2.5 W add a bias winding with a standard-recovery rectifier (1N4003 to 1N4007) acting as a clamp, which can also feed BYPASS through a resistor, turning off the internal high-voltage current source and cutting dissipation and no-load power; above 2.5 W fit an RCD or Zener clamp. Keep the peak drain voltage at worst-case high line below BVDSS, ideally at or below 650 V.

VOR, the reflected output voltage, is the output voltage plus the output diode drop, carried to the primary by the turns ratio while the diode conducts. It adds to the DC bus and the leakage spike to make the peak drain voltage.

Cycle skipping can put audio-band energy into the transformer. Keeping peak core flux density under 1500 gauss (150 mT) and dip varnishing the transformer practically removes it. Vacuum impregnation reduces noise no better than dip varnishing; it adds winding capacitance, which helps a clampless design, but can disturb the transformer's mechanical build, especially with shield windings. Higher flux densities raise the power from a given core above the transformer power capability table but need checking for noise on production transformer samples. Z5U and similar ceramic capacitors in a clamp can also sing; a film or other dielectric is the suggested replacement.

Use a slow rectifier on the bias winding, for example a 1N400x: it filters out the leakage spike, which a fast-recovery diode would pass into the regulation error. In clampless designs the slow diode is required.

For the P, G and D packages with an HV DC input stage, the hatched SOURCE copper is made as large as possible for heat sinking. Ground the SOURCE copper to the input filter capacitor at a single point. Place the BYPASS capacitor right beside its BYPASS and SOURCE pins. Make the loop of input filter capacitor, transformer primary and the chip as small as possible. An external clamp (RCD, or a Zener of about 200 V with a diode, across the primary) needs short paths to the transformer and the chip to keep EMI down.

The copper under the chip is both the single-point ground and the heat sink; since it is the quiet SOURCE node, make it as large as possible, and likewise at the output diode cathode. Connect the Y capacitor straight from the positive terminal of the primary input filter capacitor to the common/return terminal of the secondary, so surge currents bypass the chip. With a pi (C, L, C) input filter, put the inductor between the negative terminals of the filter capacitors. Keep the loop of secondary winding, output diode and output capacitor small, and give both diode terminals copper for cooling: more at the quiet cathode, since a large anode area raises radiated EMI.

Verify on the bench under worst case: drain voltage no more than 650 V at highest input and peak overload power, keeping 50 V below the 700 V BVDSS; at highest ambient, highest input and peak overload, drain current waveforms free of transformer saturation and of excessive leading-edge spikes at start-up and in steady state, with the spike already under ILIMIT(MIN) by the time tLEB(MIN) ends and drain current always inside the absolute maximum ratings; at maximum output power, lowest input and highest ambient, temperatures of the chip, transformer, output diode and capacitors within limits, with margin for RDS(ON) spread — a SOURCE pin temperature of at most 100 °C at low line and full power is recommended.
